messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Thompson is a 65-year-old prosecutor who has experienced significant psychological distress following an incident involving police violence during his line of work. The trauma he endured has left him feeling constantly on edge and struggling with the everyday reminders that have become overwhelming triggers for him. The traumatic event occurred several months ago when Mr. Thompson was investigating a high-profile case. During a routine meeting, he found himself in a room where tensions escalated rapidly. A group of officers, acting under intense pressure from their superiors, turned hostile towards him. The situation quickly spiraled out of control, with Mr. Thompson enduring both verbal and physical abuse. He vividly recalls the incomprehensible chatter and aggressive posturing of the officers as they encircled him, making him feel trapped and threatened. Since then, Mr. Thompson has found that his symptoms have steadily worsened. The moral violation he experienced during the incident has left him particularly sensitive to any signs of misbehavior or misconduct from others. Even the presence of authority figures, especially those in uniform, brings back vivid memories of that traumatic event. He now constantly scans his surroundings for any sign of threat and watches other people closely, always on guard. His heightened sense of vigilance is a direct response to these triggers. For instance, whenever he hears incomprehensible chatter or sees police presence, the memory of the incident resurfaces with startling clarity, heightening his anxiety. This has led him to adopt several maladaptive strategies to cope with his distress. He often puts on loud music or TV to distract himself from these overwhelming sensations and frequently seeks reassurance from his wife that he is safe. The constant need for this reassurance and the sensory distractions have become an ingrained part of his daily routine. These maladaptive strategies, however, have only served to perpetuate his cycle of fear and hypervigilance. By engaging in these behaviors, Mr. Thompson inadvertently reinforces his perception of threat. For example, the loud music he uses as a distraction often leads him to be more alert to sudden noises or changes in his environment, making it difficult for him to relax or fall asleep at night. His relationship with his wife has also been affected by this cycle. She notices that he is always on edge and feels like she needs to constantly reassure him, which places additional stress on their daily interactions. At work, Mr. Thompson's hypervigilance and constant scanning of the environment have made it challenging for him to focus on his cases, leading to a decline in his performance. The combination of these maladaptive strategies and heightened threat perception has created a reinforcing loop that continues to tighten over time. His persistent need for sensory distraction and reassurance further exacerbates his fear responses, making even minor triggers more potent. It was the increasing severity of these symptoms and their impact on both his professional and personal life that finally prompted Mr. Thompson to seek help. He is most afraid of being unable to fulfill his responsibilities as a prosecutor and maintaining healthy relationships with his family. What he hopes for is finding a way to reclaim control over his life and reduce the overwhelming sense of threat that has come to define his daily existence.
